units.title: Counting the Pennies
units.caption: A furnished flat. The day before Christmas.
stanzas:
One dollar and eighty-seven cents.
That was all.
And sixty cents of it was in pennies.
Pennies saved one and two at a time
by {bulldozing|pushing and bullying} the grocer and the vegetable man and the butcher
until one’s cheeks burned with the silent {imputation|unspoken accusation} of {parsimony|being mean with money}
that such close dealing implied.
Three times Della counted it.
One dollar and eighty-seven cents.
And the next day would be Christmas.

There was clearly nothing to do
but flop down on the {shabby|old and worn out} little couch and {howl|cry very loudly}.
So Della did it.
Which {instigates|starts, sets going} the moral reflection
that life is made up of sobs, sniffles, and smiles,
with sniffles {predominating|being the biggest part}.
units.para: Della has saved money for months — and she has only one dollar and eighty-seven cents. Most of it is small pennies, saved by arguing over every price until the shopkeepers silently thought she was cheap. She counts it three times. Tomorrow is Christmas. So she falls on the old couch and cries.

units.title: The Eight-Dollar Flat
units.caption: A letter-box that takes no letters. A bell that will not ring.
stanzas:
While the mistress of the home is gradually {subsiding|calming down, sinking} from the first stage to the second,
take a look at the home.
A furnished flat at $8 per week.
It did not exactly {beggar|be too poor for} description,
but it certainly had that word on the lookout for the {mendicancy|begging} squad.

In the {vestibule|a small entrance hall} below was a letter-box into which no letter would go,
and an electric button from which no {mortal|human} finger could {coax|gently persuade} a ring.
Also appertaining thereunto was a card bearing the name
“Mr. James Dillingham Young.”

The “Dillingham” had been flung to the breeze
during a former period of {prosperity|good times, having money}
when its possessor was being paid $30 per week.
Now, when the income was shrunk to $20, though,
they were thinking seriously of contracting to a modest and unassuming D.
But whenever Mr. James Dillingham Young came home and reached his flat above
he was called “Jim” and greatly hugged by Mrs. James Dillingham Young,
already introduced to you as Della.
Which is all very good.
units.para: While Della cries, the narrator shows us the home: a rented flat for eight dollars a week, close to real poverty. Downstairs, a broken letter-box and a doorbell that does not work — and a proud name card: Mr. James Dillingham Young. Jim put up the long name when he earned thirty dollars a week. Now he earns twenty. But every evening, Della hugs him at the door and calls him Jim — and that, the narrator says, is all very good.

units.title: The Gray Cat and the Glass
units.caption: A window, a mirror, and a decision arriving.
stanzas:
Della finished her cry and attended to her cheeks with the powder rag.
She stood by the window and looked out dully
at a gray cat walking a gray fence in a gray backyard.
Tomorrow would be Christmas Day,
and she had only $1.87 with which to buy Jim a present.
She had been saving every penny she could for months, with this result.
Twenty dollars a week doesn’t go far.
Expenses had been greater than she had calculated.
They always are.
Only $1.87 to buy a present for Jim. Her Jim.
Many a happy hour she had spent planning for something nice for him.
Something fine and rare and {sterling|of true, solid quality}—
something just a little bit near to being worthy of the honor
of being owned by Jim.

There was a {pier glass|a tall narrow mirror} between the windows of the room.
Perhaps you have seen a pier glass in an $8 flat.
A very thin and very {agile|quick and light in movement} person may,
by observing his reflection in a rapid sequence of {longitudinal|up-and-down, lengthwise} strips,
obtain a fairly accurate conception of his looks.
Della, being slender, had mastered the art.

Suddenly she whirled from the window and stood before the glass.
Her eyes were shining {brilliantly|very brightly},
but her face had lost its color within twenty seconds.
Rapidly she pulled down her hair
and let it fall to its full length.
units.para: Della dries her eyes and looks out at a gray, dull world. She has planned for months to buy Jim something fine and rare — something good enough for him — and she has $1.87. Then, suddenly, she turns to the narrow mirror between the windows. Her eyes are shining, but her face goes pale: she has had an idea, and the idea costs something. She pulls down her hair and lets it fall.

units.title: The Two Treasures
units.caption: A gold watch, and hair like brown water.
stanzas:
Now, there were two possessions of the James Dillingham Youngs
in which they both took a mighty pride.
One was Jim’s gold watch that had been his father’s and his grandfather’s.
The other was Della’s hair.
Had the queen of Sheba lived in the flat across the {airshaft|a narrow open space between buildings},
Della would have let her hair hang out the window some day to dry
just to {depreciate|make something seem less valuable} Her Majesty’s jewels and gifts.
Had King Solomon been the {janitor|a building caretaker},
with all his treasures piled up in the basement,
Jim would have pulled out his watch every time he passed,
just to see him {pluck|pull sharply} at his beard from envy.

So now Della’s beautiful hair fell about her
rippling and shining like a {cascade|a small waterfall} of brown waters.
It reached below her knee
and made itself almost a garment for her.
And then she did it up again nervously and quickly.
Once she {faltered|paused, almost stopped} for a minute and stood still
while a tear or two splashed on the worn red carpet.
units.para: The couple owns two treasures. Jim's gold watch, passed down from his grandfather and father. And Della's hair, which falls below her knee like a waterfall of brown water. The narrator says even the richest queen and king in old stories would have envied them. Della lets her hair down, looks at it — then puts it up again, quickly. She stops once. Two tears fall on the worn carpet. She has decided.
gloss: a narrow open space between buildings

units.title: Madame Sofronie
units.caption: One flight up. Hair goods of all kinds.
stanzas:
On went her old brown jacket; on went her old brown hat.
With a whirl of skirts and with the brilliant sparkle still in her eyes,
she {fluttered|moved quickly and lightly} out the door and down the stairs to the street.

Where she stopped the sign read:
“Mme. Sofronie. Hair Goods of All Kinds.”
One flight up Della ran, and collected herself, {panting|breathing hard and fast}.
Madame, large, too white, {chilly|cold in manner}, hardly looked the “Sofronie.”

“Will you buy my hair?” asked Della.
“I buy hair,” said Madame.
“Take yer hat off and let’s have a sight at the looks of it.”
Down rippled the brown cascade.
“Twenty dollars,” said Madame, lifting the mass with a {practised|skilled from much repeating} hand.
“Give it to me quick,” said Della.
units.para: Della puts on her old brown jacket and hat and hurries into the street. She finds a shop sign: Mme. Sofronie — Hair Goods of All Kinds. The owner is large, pale, and cold. Della asks: "Will you buy my hair?" The woman looks, lifts the brown waterfall with an expert hand, and says: twenty dollars. Della does not stop to think. "Give it to me quick."

units.title: The Chain
units.caption: Two hours on rosy wings. Then, in a shop window—
stanzas:
Oh, and the next two hours tripped by on rosy wings.
Forget the {hashed|mixed-up, overused} metaphor.
She was {ransacking|searching wildly through} the stores for Jim’s present.

She found it at last.
It surely had been made for Jim and no one else.
There was no other like it in any of the stores,
and she had turned all of them inside out.
It was a platinum {fob chain|a short chain for a pocket watch} simple and {chaste|plain and pure in style} in design,
properly proclaiming its value by substance alone
and not by {meretricious|falsely attractive, showy} ornamentation—
as all good things should do.
It was even worthy of The Watch.
As soon as she saw it she knew that it must be Jim’s.
It was like him.
Quietness and value—the description applied to both.
Twenty-one dollars they took from her for it,
and she hurried home with the 87 cents.
With that chain on his watch
Jim might be properly anxious about the time in any company.
Grand as the watch was,
he sometimes looked at it on the sly
on account of the old leather strap that he used in place of a chain.
units.para: For two happy hours Della searches every store in town. At last she finds it: a platinum chain for Jim's pocket watch — simple, plain, valuable for what it is, not for show. "Quietness and value" — like Jim himself. It costs twenty-one dollars. She goes home with 87 cents. Now Jim can proudly check the time in front of anyone — until now, he sometimes looked at his grand watch secretly, because it hung on an old leather strap.
gloss: a short chain for a pocket watch

units.title: The Curls
units.caption: Curling irons, and forty minutes of repair.
stanzas:
When Della reached home
her {intoxication|great excitement, like being drunk on joy} gave way a little to {prudence|careful good sense} and reason.
She got out her curling irons and lighted the gas
and went to work repairing the {ravages|serious damage} made by generosity added to love.
Which is always a tremendous task, dear friends—
a {mammoth|huge} task.

Within forty minutes her head was covered with tiny, close-lying curls
that made her look wonderfully like a {truant|staying away from school without permission} schoolboy.
She looked at her reflection in the mirror
long, carefully, and critically.

“If Jim doesn’t kill me,” she said to herself,
“before he takes a second look at me,
he’ll say I look like a Coney Island chorus girl.
But what could I do—oh!
what could I do with a dollar and eighty-seven cents?”
units.para: At home, the excitement fades and worry arrives. Della heats her curling irons and spends forty minutes repairing what love has done. Now her head is covered in tiny curls, like a schoolboy's. She studies the mirror and tells herself: Jim will say I look like a cheap dancer. But what could I do with a dollar and eighty-seven cents?
gloss: great excitement, like being drunk on joy
staying away from school without permission

units.title: The Stare
units.caption: Seven o'clock. A step on the stair.
stanzas:
At 7 o’clock the coffee was made
and the frying-pan was on the back of the stove
hot and ready to cook the chops.

Jim was never late.
Della doubled the fob chain in her hand
and sat on the corner of the table near the door that he always entered.
Then she heard his step on the stair away down on the first flight,
and she turned white for just a moment.
She had a habit of saying a little silent prayer
about the simplest everyday things,
and now she whispered:
“Please God, make him think I am still pretty.”

The door opened and Jim stepped in and closed it.
He looked thin and very serious.
Poor fellow, he was only twenty-two—
and to be burdened with a family!
He needed a new overcoat and he was without gloves.

Jim stopped inside the door,
as {immovable|unable to be moved} as a {setter|a hunting dog that freezes when it finds a bird} at the scent of {quail|a small game bird},
His eyes were fixed upon Della,
and there was an expression in them that she could not read,
and it terrified her.
It was not anger, nor surprise, nor {disapproval|thinking something is wrong or bad}, nor horror,
nor any of the {sentiments|feelings} that she had been prepared for.
He simply stared at her fixedly
with that {peculiar|strange, unusual} expression on his face.
units.para: Seven o'clock. Coffee ready, pan hot. Della sits by the door with the chain in her hand and whispers a small prayer: "Please God, make him think I am still pretty." Jim comes in — thin, serious, only twenty-two, needing a new coat, with no gloves. And then he stops. He stares at her with an expression she cannot read. Not anger. Not surprise. Not horror. Something else — and it frightens her.
gloss: a hunting dog that freezes when it finds a bird
thinking something is wrong or bad

units.title: Sold and Gone
units.caption: “It went for you.”
stanzas:
Della wriggled off the table and went for him.
“Jim, darling,” she cried, “don’t look at me that way.
I had my hair cut off and sold
because I couldn’t have lived through Christmas
without giving you a present.
It’ll grow out again—you won’t mind, will you?
I just had to do it.
My hair grows awfully fast.
Say ‘Merry Christmas!’ Jim, and let’s be happy.
You don’t know what a nice—
what a beautiful, nice gift I’ve got for you.”

“You’ve cut off your hair?” asked Jim, {laboriously|slowly, with great effort},
as if he had not arrived at that {patent|obvious} fact yet
even after the hardest mental labor.
“Cut it off and sold it,” said Della.
“Don’t you like me just as well, anyhow?
I’m me without my hair, ain’t I?”
Jim looked about the room curiously.
“You say your hair is gone?” he said,
with an air almost of {idiocy|foolishness, not thinking clearly}.

“You needn’t look for it,” said Della.
“It’s sold, I tell you—sold and gone, too.
It’s Christmas Eve, boy. Be good to me, for it went for you.
Maybe the hairs of my head were numbered,” she went on with sudden serious sweetness,
“but nobody could ever count my love for you.
Shall I put the chops on, Jim?”

Out of his {trance|a state of staring without seeing} Jim seemed quickly to wake.
He {enfolded|wrapped his arms around} his Della.
For ten seconds let us regard with {discreet|politely careful} {scrutiny|close examination}
some inconsequential object in the other direction.
Eight dollars a week or a million a year—
what is the difference?
A mathematician or a wit would give you the wrong answer.
The magi brought valuable gifts, but that was not among them.
This dark assertion will be illuminated later on.
units.para: Della runs to him: I sold my hair — I couldn't live through Christmas without giving you a present. Jim asks again and again, slowly, as if the fact will not enter his head: "You've cut off your hair?" Della answers: sold and gone — it went for you — and no one could ever count my love. Jim wakes from his trance and holds her. The narrator looks politely away, and asks a strange question: eight dollars a week or a million a year — what is the difference? The answer, he says, will come later.
gloss: a state of staring without seeing

units.title: The Combs
units.caption: A package on the table.
stanzas:
Jim drew a package from his overcoat pocket
and threw it upon the table.
“Don’t make any mistake, Dell,” he said, “about me.
I don’t think there’s anything in the way of a haircut or a shave or a shampoo
that could make me like my girl any less.
But if you’ll unwrap that package
you may see why you had me going a while at first.”

White fingers and {nimble|quick and skilful} tore at the string and paper.
And then an {ecstatic|full of overwhelming joy} scream of joy;
and then, alas! a quick feminine change to hysterical tears and wails,
necessitating the immediate employment
of all the comforting powers of the lord of the flat.

For there lay The Combs—the set of combs, side and back,
that Della had {worshipped|loved and admired like something holy} long in a Broadway window.
Beautiful combs, pure tortoise shell, with jewelled rims—
just the shade to wear in the beautiful vanished hair.
They were expensive combs, she knew,
and her heart had simply {craved|wanted painfully} and {yearned|longed deeply} over them
without the least hope of possession.
And now, they were hers,
but the {tresses|long locks of hair} that should have adorned the {coveted|badly wanted} adornments were gone.

But she hugged them to her bosom,
and at length she was able to look up with dim eyes and a smile and say:
“My hair grows so fast, Jim!”
And then Della leaped up like a little singed cat and cried, “Oh, oh!”
units.para: Jim puts a package on the table: nothing could make me like my girl any less — but open it, and you'll see why I stared. Della tears the paper — a scream of joy — then tears. Inside are The Combs: the beautiful tortoise-shell combs she had admired in a shop window for months without any hope of owning them. Combs for hair that is gone. She hugs them, smiles through wet eyes — "My hair grows so fast, Jim!" — and then suddenly jumps up. She has remembered her own present.
gloss: loved and admired like something holy

units.title: The Watch
units.caption: An open palm. A dull precious shine.
stanzas:
Jim had not yet seen his beautiful present.
She held it out to him eagerly upon her open palm.
The dull precious metal seemed to flash
with a reflection of her bright and {ardent|burning with feeling} spirit.

“Isn’t it a dandy, Jim?
I hunted all over town to find it.
You’ll have to look at the time a hundred times a day now.
Give me your watch.
I want to see how it looks on it.”

Instead of obeying, Jim tumbled down on the couch
and put his hands under the back of his head and smiled.
“Dell,” said he, “let’s put our Christmas presents away
and keep ’em a while.
They’re too nice to use just at present.
I sold the watch to get the money to buy your combs.
And now suppose you put the chops on.”
units.para: Della holds out the chain on her open hand: "Give me your watch. I want to see how it looks on it." Jim does not reach for his watch. He lies back on the couch and smiles: let's put our presents away for a while — they're too nice to use just now. "I sold the watch to get the money to buy your combs." And then, gently: now suppose you put the chops on.

units.title: The Wisest
units.caption: The narrator turns to face you.
stanzas:
The magi, as you know, were wise men—wonderfully wise men—
who brought gifts to the Babe in the {manger|a food box for animals, used as a bed}.
They invented the art of giving Christmas presents.
Being wise, their gifts were no doubt wise ones,
possibly bearing the privilege of exchange in case of {duplication|two of the same thing}.
And here I have lamely related to you
the uneventful {chronicle|a record of events} of two foolish children in a flat
who most unwisely {sacrificed|gave up something precious} for each other
the greatest treasures of their house.
But in a last word to the wise of these days
let it be said that of all who give gifts
these two were the wisest.
Of all who give and receive gifts, such as they are wisest.
Everywhere they are wisest.
They are the magi.
units.para: The narrator ends by talking about the magi — the wise men who brought the first Christmas gifts. Their gifts were wise ones. And these two "foolish children" gave up the greatest treasures they had, for each other — hair for a watch that is sold, a chain for hair that is gone. Foolish? The narrator says the opposite: of all who give gifts, these two were the wisest. They are the magi.
gloss: a food box for animals, used as a bed

s1.watch: A tiny flat, the day before Christmas, and a woman counting her money. Watch the number. Just watch.
s1.focus: Listen for how many times she counts the money. And notice how those pennies were saved — it cost her something besides time.

debrief.ok: Yes — three times. The number will not change, and she counts it anyway. That is what hope looks like when it is losing.
debrief.no: 'Three times Della counted it.' Counting again cannot make it grow — and that is exactly why the next thing she does is cry.

s1.writeIntro: This one asks for feelings. Say how Della feels, then use the number itself as your evidence — it is the best evidence in the whole scene.

mc.q: How much money has Della saved for Jim's present?
opts: Eight dollars, the weekly rent
One dollar and eighty-seven cents
Twenty dollars, Jim's whole weekly pay
Sixty cents in pennies
mc.fb: 'One dollar and eighty-seven cents. That was all.' The sixty cents in pennies is only part of it, and eight and twenty dollars are the rent and Jim's pay.

mc.q: Why did saving the pennies make Della's cheeks burn?
opts: She was ashamed that the shopkeepers silently thought she was mean with money.
She had to run from shop to shop in the cold looking for the lowest prices.
The grocer shouted at her in front of the other customers.
She was embarrassed to pay for food with handfuls of pennies.
mc.fb: Her cheeks burned with 'the silent imputation of parsimony' — the unspoken accusation of being cheap. Nobody shouted; the shame was in what the shopkeepers were silently thinking.

sa.q: Why does Della cry? Use the number and the day in your answer.
sa.hint: Feelings first: sad? hopeless? Then the facts — how much she has, and what tomorrow is.
phrases: the next day would be christmas

s2.watch: She is still crying. So the narrator does a strange thing — he walks us downstairs to look at the building. Look at what is broken.
s2.focus: The narrator makes a joke about a name card. Listen for two numbers — what Jim used to earn, and what he earns now.

debrief.ok: Right — thirty down to twenty. The name got long when the money was good, and now the pride is shrinking along with the pay.
debrief.no: The card went up when Jim was 'paid $30 per week', and now 'the income was shrunk to $20'. The proud long name is shrinking with the money.

s2.writeIntro: Two-part answer: what the long name card meant when it went up, and what it means now that the money is smaller. The card tells you both.

mc.q: Why are they thinking of shortening 'Dillingham' to a modest 'D'?
opts: Jim's pay has dropped from thirty dollars a week to twenty.
The old card is too large to fit in the little letter-box downstairs.
Della has always thought the long name sounded silly.
A new neighbor has put up a card with the same name.
mc.fb: The long name was 'flung to the breeze' at $30 a week; 'now, when the income was shrunk to $20', it feels too grand. The name stretched with the money and shrinks with it.

mc.q: The narrator ends the scene with 'Which is all very good.' What is all very good?
opts: The flat, which the narrator thinks is comfortable enough for eight dollars a week.
That Della hugs Jim and calls him Jim every evening, whatever the card says.
The name card, which still looks proud and fine in the vestibule.
Jim's plan to earn thirty dollars a week again someday.
mc.fb: Whenever Jim comes home he is 'called Jim and greatly hugged'. After a whole paragraph about broken things and shrinking money, the narrator points at the one thing that still works.

sa.q: The narrator jokes about the name card. What did the long name 'Mr. James Dillingham Young' show about Jim when he put it up — and what has changed since?
sa.hint: Think about pride and pay. Thirty dollars then, twenty now — and what still waits for him at the top of the stairs.

s3.watch: She is done crying now. Watch the window first, then the mirror. Something happens in her face — do not miss it.
s3.focus: Count how many gray things she sees out the window. Then watch her face at the mirror — two opposite things happen to it at the same time.

debrief.ok: Yes — shining eyes and a pale face, in the same twenty seconds. She has had an idea, and the idea costs something.
debrief.no: 'Her eyes were shining brilliantly, but her face had lost its color.' Excitement and fear at once — she has just decided something.

s3.writeIntro: You are reading her body here, not her words. Name both feelings — the bright one and the frightened one — and then make your guess at the plan.

mc.q: What does Della see when she looks out the window?
opts: A gray cat walking a gray fence in a gray backyard.
Snow beginning to fall on the empty street below.
Jim walking home early along the darkening street.
The bright windows of the shops where she wanted to buy his present.
mc.fb: 'A gray cat walking a gray fence in a gray backyard.' Gray three times in one line — the world outside is offering her exactly nothing.

mc.q: At the mirror, what happens to Della within twenty seconds?
opts: Her eyes shine, but her face loses its color.
She begins to cry again and turns away from the glass.
She smiles at herself and starts fixing her hat to go out.
She counts her money one more time in front of the mirror.
mc.fb: 'Her eyes were shining brilliantly, but her face had lost its color within twenty seconds.' The crying is finished — this is something new: excitement and fear arriving together.

sa.q: Della has not told us her plan, but her body has. What do her shining eyes and her pale face tell you she is feeling? Then guess what she has decided to do.
sa.hint: Two feelings at once — one bright, one frightened. Then look at what her hands do with her hair.

s4.watch: The story stops for a moment, and the narrator shows us the two most precious things in this flat. Listen for what they are.
s4.focus: The narrator brings in a queen and a king from very old stories. Listen for why — what would those rich royals feel if they saw Jim's watch and Della's hair?

debrief.ok: Yes — envy. A queen jealous of hair, a king jealous of a watch. The narrator is exaggerating on purpose, boasting for his two poor friends.
debrief.no: Jim would show the watch 'just to see him pluck at his beard from envy.' It is a friendly exaggeration: these two poor people own things kings and queens would want.

s4.writeIntro: Feelings first. Then say what letting her hair down, putting it up again quickly, and those two tears tell you she has decided to do.

mc.q: What are the two treasures of the James Dillingham Youngs?
opts: Jim's gold watch and Della's hair.
The proud name card and the gold watch.
Della's hair and her grandmother's ring.
The furnished flat and Jim's weekly pay.
mc.fb: 'One was Jim's gold watch that had been his father's and his grandfather's. The other was Della's hair.' Not things they bought — things that are part of who they are.

mc.q: Why does the narrator bring in the queen of Sheba and King Solomon?
opts: To exaggerate in fun: even the richest royals would envy these two treasures.
To show that the story really takes place in ancient times, long before this Christmas.
Because Della often dreams of being as rich as a famous queen.
Because a king and a queen once lived in the flat across the airshaft.
mc.fb: Sheba's 'jewels and gifts' would look smaller next to Della's hair, and Solomon would 'pluck at his beard from envy' of the watch. It is playful exaggeration — the narrator boasting for two people with a broken doorbell.

sa.q: Della lets her hair fall down, then puts it up again quickly — and a tear or two splashes on the carpet. What is she feeling, and why?
sa.hint: Feelings first: what does it cost to say goodbye to your treasure? Then say who she is doing it for.

s5.watch: She has decided. Now watch how fast she moves — the speed is the whole point of this part.
s5.focus: Listen for the last thing Della says in the shop. It is only five words, and one of them matters more than the price.

debrief.ok: Yes. 'Give it to me quick.' If she stands there holding her own hair, she has time to change her mind.
debrief.no: 'Give it to me quick.' She is not bargaining and she is not in a hurry to shop — she wants the money in her hand before she can change her mind.

s5.writeIntro: Two people are looking at the same hair in this scene, and it means something completely different to each of them. Show both sides.

mc.q: How does Madame Sofronie treat Della's beautiful hair?
opts: She admires it and says it is the finest hair she has ever bought.
She weighs it like goods and names a price.
She refuses it at first, to push the price down lower.
She asks Della why a poor woman would ever sell such a treasure.
mc.fb: She lifts 'the mass with a practised hand' and says 'Twenty dollars.' To her it is stock for the shop — hair goods of all kinds.

mc.q: Why does Della say 'Give it to me quick'?
opts: So she cannot stop and change her mind.
Because Madame Sofronie told her to hurry up.
Because the shop is about to close for Christmas Eve.
Because she is frightened of the large, cold shop owner.
mc.fb: 'Give it to me quick.' If she waits even a minute, she has time to remember what she is selling. Speed is how she protects the decision.

sa.q: Madame is 'chilly' and lifts the hair with a 'practised hand'. Della's eyes are sparkling. Explain what the hair means to each of these two women.
sa.hint: For one of them it is business — goods with a price. For the other it is a treasure, and the only way to buy Jim's present.

s6.watch: Two hours of searching every store in town — and then one shop window. Watch what she finds, and why she knows it is right.
s6.focus: The narrator describes the chain with two words that could just as easily describe a person. Listen for them.

debrief.ok: Yes — 'Quietness and value'. The chain is not just a present. It is a small portrait of Jim.
debrief.no: 'Quietness and value — the description applied to both.' Both — the chain and Jim. She is not buying jewellery; she is buying his likeness.

s6.writeIntro: There is a small, sad detail hiding at the end of this part: a grand watch on an old leather strap. Explain what that strap does to Jim.

mc.q: Why does Della know at once that the chain 'must be Jim's'?
opts: It is the most expensive chain in any of the stores.
It is covered in fine, showy ornament, like a rich man's chain.
It is quiet and valuable, like Jim himself.
It matches the old leather strap that Jim already uses.
mc.fb: 'It was like him. Quietness and value—the description applied to both.' Plain, real, and worth more than it shows — that is the chain, and that is Jim.

mc.q: Why does Jim sometimes look at his grand watch 'on the sly'?
opts: He is ashamed of the old leather strap it hangs on.
He is afraid that someone in the street will steal it.
He does not want Della to know that he still carries it.
Looking at a watch during work is against his employer's rules.
mc.fb: 'On account of the old leather strap that he used in place of a chain.' The watch is grand; the strap says poor. So he checks the time secretly.

sa.q: Jim owns a grand gold watch, but he checks it secretly. Explain why — and what Della's chain will change for him.
sa.hint: Think about pride and shame. The watch is grand; the strap is old leather. With the chain, what can he do 'in any company'?

s7.watch: She is home, and the excitement is wearing off. Watch what forty minutes of work with the curling irons turns her into.
s7.focus: At the mirror, Della asks herself one question — twice. Listen for it. You have heard the number inside it before.

debrief.ok: Yes. 'What could I do with a dollar and eighty-seven cents?' That number opened the story — and it drives every choice she makes.
debrief.no: 'What could I do — oh! what could I do with a dollar and eighty-seven cents?' It is the same money from part one. The whole story runs on that question.

s7.writeIntro: She is worried about how she looks — but ask yourself who she is worried FOR. That is the real question here.

mc.q: What does Della do for forty minutes when she reaches home?
opts: She wraps Jim's present carefully in paper and string.
She cooks the chops and makes the coffee for Jim's dinner.
She curls what is left of her hair.
She counts her last eighty-seven cents again and again.
mc.fb: She goes 'to work repairing the ravages made by generosity added to love'. Curling irons, gas, forty minutes — and tiny, close-lying curls.

mc.q: When Della asks the mirror 'what could I do?', what is she really telling herself?
opts: That she should have asked Jim before she sold her hair.
That there was no other way to give Jim a present.
That Madame Sofronie paid her far too little for it.
That the eighty-seven cents might still buy her a wig.
mc.fb: 'What could I do with a dollar and eighty-seven cents?' It is not an excuse — it is the plain truth, and it is the engine of the whole story.

sa.q: Della is afraid Jim will say she looks 'like a Coney Island chorus girl'. Is she worried about being pretty for her own sake — or for something else? Explain, using the text.
sa.hint: She did not cut her hair for fashion. Whose opinion is she afraid of tonight — and why does that one opinion matter so much?

s8.watch: Seven o'clock. Coffee made, pan hot, chain in her hand. Watch Jim's face when the door opens — and watch what it does NOT show.
s8.focus: Della has prepared herself for certain feelings on Jim's face. Listen for the list of everything his stare is NOT.

debrief.ok: Yes — not anger, not surprise, not disapproval, not horror. She had an answer ready for every one of those. This is something else.
debrief.no: 'It was not anger, nor surprise, nor disapproval, nor horror.' She prepared for all of those. For this stare she has nothing — and neither do we, yet.

s8.writeIntro: Before the stare, the narrator stops the scene for three small facts about Jim. Poor facts. Collect them — the story is going to need them.

mc.q: What does the narrator tell us about Jim as he comes in?
opts: He is twenty-two, needs a new overcoat, and has no gloves.
He is smiling, and hiding a Christmas package behind his back for Della.
He is angry with Della even before he has opened the door of the flat.
He has been paid thirty dollars a week again and looks well dressed.
mc.fb: 'He needed a new overcoat and he was without gloves.' Only twenty-two, and burdened with a family. Note it quietly: Jim is exactly as poor as Della.

mc.q: Why does Jim's stare terrify Della?
opts: It is plainly full of anger about the money she has spent.
It shows open horror at her tiny short curls.
It is a feeling she cannot read or name.
He looks straight past her, as if she were not in the room at all.
mc.fb: 'An expression in them that she could not read.' Not anger, nor surprise, nor horror — she was ready for those. This is something with no name yet.

sa.q: 'Please God, make him think I am still pretty.' What is Della really asking for in this little prayer? Explain it in your own words.
sa.hint: It is not about mirrors. It is about Jim — what she is afraid of losing, and who she gave her hair away for.

s9.watch: Della rushes to explain. Watch Jim — he is strangely slow, and it is not anger.
s9.focus: Watch Jim while Della talks. He keeps asking one question, very slowly. Decide what that slowness means.

debrief.ok: Yes — he is not angry. The fact simply will not go into his head, and there is a reason for that we cannot see yet.
debrief.no: Look at 'laboriously' — slowly, with great effort. He asks 'You've cut off your hair?' again and again. That is not anger. Something else is blocking his mind.

s9.writeIntro: You are explaining Della's best sentence. Say what she means in plain words first, then say why 'counting' is exactly the right idea for it.

mc.q: What does Jim keep asking Della, slowly, again and again?
opts: Why she spent all of their saved money.
Whether her hair is really gone.
Who cut her hair off for her.
Where she has hidden his present.
mc.fb: 'You say your hair is gone?' He asks it 'laboriously', as if the obvious fact will not enter his head. Remember this look — it is explained in the next part.

mc.q: The narrator asks: eight dollars a week or a million a year — what is the difference? What is he telling us?
opts: A mathematician could calculate the difference exactly.
The money means nothing next to what these two have.
Jim will be earning a million a year one day.
Poor families are always happier than rich ones.
mc.fb: 'A mathematician or a wit would give you the wrong answer.' Whatever Della and Jim hold in that hug, no amount of money measures it.

sa.q: Della says maybe the hairs of her head were numbered, 'but nobody could ever count my love for you.' Explain in your own words what she means.
sa.hint: Hairs can be counted — they come to an end. What about her love? Simple words work: big, endless, more than, cannot be measured.

s10.watch: Jim has brought a present too. Watch Della's face change twice.
s10.focus: The package explains the stare at the door. When Della opens it, ask yourself: why is this exact gift the one that hurts?

debrief.ok: Yes. The combs are perfect for the one treasure she no longer has. Now Jim's stare at the door finally makes sense.
debrief.no: The combs were 'just the shade to wear in the beautiful vanished hair'. They fit the treasure that is gone — that is why joy turns to tears in one second.

s10.writeIntro: Two small moments to explain here: what makes Della jump up at the very end, and what she has suddenly remembered. Tell me both.

mc.q: Della gives a scream of joy — and one second later she is crying. Why?
opts: The combs are broken inside the paper.
The combs are for the hair she no longer has.
Jim has spent the rent money that they needed.
She had wanted a different set of combs.
mc.fb: They are 'just the shade to wear in the beautiful vanished hair'. The perfect gift arrived one day after the hair it was made for.

mc.q: Why does Della look up, smile, and say 'My hair grows so fast, Jim!'?
opts: She is being brave, for Jim's sake.
She truly believes her hair will be back before New Year.
She wants Jim to take the combs back to the shop.
She is secretly angry and hiding it from him.
mc.fb: She says it 'with dim eyes and a smile' — through tears. The combs fit hair that is gone, so she gives Jim the only comfort she can find.

sa.q: At the very end Della leaps up 'like a little singed cat' and cries 'Oh, oh!' What has she suddenly remembered, and why does she jump?
sa.hint: She has been crying over Jim's gift to her. But there is a second present in this room — whose is it, and has Jim seen it yet?

s11.watch: Della still thinks the chain has a home to go to. Watch Jim's smile — he knows something she doesn't, one last time.
s11.focus: Della asks for the watch. Listen for Jim's answer — it is one flat, quiet sentence, and it changes everything.

debrief.ok: Yes. No speech, no tears — one plain sentence, a smile, and then dinner. The story trusts you to feel it without any help.
debrief.no: 'I sold the watch to get the money to buy your combs.' That is the whole reveal — said quietly, from the couch, with a smile.

s11.writeIntro: Explain why neither present can be used tonight. Take the gifts one at a time: what each one needs, and what has happened to that thing.

mc.q: How does Jim tell Della that the watch is gone?
opts: He cries and says that he is sorry.
With a smile, in one calm sentence.
He silently shows her his empty watch pocket.
He waits until after dinner to tell her the truth.
mc.fb: He 'tumbled down on the couch' and smiled: 'I sold the watch to get the money to buy your combs.' No drama at all — that is the point.

mc.q: What does Jim ask Della to do, right after the truth is out?
opts: Put the chops on.
Try the combs in what is left of her hair.
Put the chain safely away in a drawer.
Promise never to sell anything again.
mc.fb: 'And now suppose you put the chops on.' Ordinary life simply continues — and that gentle, everyday sentence may be the tenderest line in the story.

sa.q: Jim says: let's put our Christmas presents away and keep them a while — 'They're too nice to use just at present.' Explain why neither gift can be used tonight. What has happened to both of them?
sa.hint: The chain was bought for the watch. The combs were bought for the hair. Where is the watch now? Where is the hair?

s12.watch: The story is over. Now the narrator stops telling it and turns to talk to you directly.
s12.focus: The narrator uses the word 'foolish' and the word 'wisest' about the same two people. Listen for how he gets from one word to the other.

debrief.ok: Yes. The gifts were foolish — the givers were the wisest. He means both things at once, and the last word of the story is its title.
debrief.no: 'Two foolish children... of all who give gifts these two were the wisest.' He says both, on purpose. The gifts failed; the giving did not.

s12.writeIntro: This is an opinion question, and both answers can be right. Call them foolish, or call them wise — either one makes a good answer, as long as you defend it with something they actually did. You can even argue both at once; the narrator does.

mc.q: Who were the original magi?
opts: Rich kings who ruled in old New York.
Shopkeepers who invented Christmas sales.
Wise men who brought gifts to the Babe in the manger.
The first children ever to receive presents.
mc.fb: 'The magi, as you know, were wise men — wonderfully wise men' who brought the first Christmas gifts. Keep that word 'wise' in view for the last line.

mc.q: What is the narrator's final judgment of Della and Jim?
opts: They were careless and should have saved their money for the rent.
Their story is too small and uneventful to teach anything.
They should have exchanged the gifts at the shops.
Of all who give gifts, they are the wisest.
mc.fb: He teases them as 'two foolish children' — then turns it around: 'of all who give gifts these two were the wisest. They are the magi.'

sa.q: So — were Della and Jim foolish, or wise? Take a side, or argue both, and defend it with what they actually did.
sa.hint: Foolish: both gifts are useless now, and the money and treasures are gone. Wise: each one gave up their best thing for the other. There is no wrong side — just give your reason.

ohenry.watch: Before the story, meet the man who wrote it. Just listen.
ohenry.focus: Listen for what happened to him in Ohio — and what name he came out with.

debrief.ok: Yes. He knew being poor, and he knew starting again. Keep both in mind while you read.
debrief.no: Go back to the Ohio years — what he lost there, and the new name he found.

ohenry.writeIntro: Say one thing about his life, then point at the part of this story it might explain.

mc.q: Where did William Sydney Porter begin publishing stories as "O. Henry"?
opts: In a New York newspaper office
While hiding in Honduras
While serving time in an Ohio prison
As a student in North Carolina
mc.fb: He wrote in his cell and mailed stories out under invented names so editors would not know the author was a prisoner. "O. Henry" first appeared in 1899.

mc.q: What deal did O. Henry have with the New York World's Sunday magazine?
opts: One story every week
One novel every year
A daily news column
He owned the magazine
mc.fb: A story a week, for over a year — one of the reasons he produced nearly 400 stories in a short life.

sa.q: O. Henry went to prison — and prison is where he became a writer. Do you think knowing about his life changes how we should read this story about poor people? Give your reason.
sa.hint: No wrong answer. Think about it: he had been poor, disgraced, and had to start again. Does that make his story about Jim and Della more honest — or does the story stand on its own?

impact.watch: The story is over. Now — why has this tiny story never died?
impact.focus: Listen for the name of the trick this story plays, and what the title has come to mean.

debrief.ok: Right. The ending surprises you, and then feels like the only ending that was ever possible.
debrief.no: Think about the two gifts once more — what each one is FOR, and what is gone.

impact.writeIntro: There is no wrong answer here. Say what you think, then hold it up against one line of the text.

mc.q: What is "situational irony", the term this story is used to teach?
opts: When a character says one thing but means another
When what happens is the opposite of what was expected
When the reader knows something the characters do not
When a story ends exactly as it began
mc.fb: Each gift was chosen for the very thing the other one sold. The outcome is the exact reverse of what both of them planned — that reversal is situational irony.

mc.q: What does it mean today to call something "a gift of the magi" situation?
opts: A gift that arrives late for Christmas
A present bought with borrowed money
An expensive gift given to a stranger
Two people each sacrificing their treasure for the other, so the gifts cancel out
mc.fb: The title became an English expression for exactly this pattern of mutual sacrifice — very few stories turn into a phrase.

sa.q: Almost everyone knows the ending of this story before they read it — and it still works. Why do you think a surprise ending can survive not being a surprise? Use the story in your answer.
sa.hint: Think about what the ending really delivers. Is it the shock — or what the two useless gifts prove about Jim and Della?

ohenry.title: O. Henry, 1862–1910
ohenry.caption: Greensboro, 1862 — New York, 1910. Forty-seven years, three names, one prison number.
spoken: His real name was William Sydney Porter. He was born in North Carolina in eighteen sixty-two, and his mother died when he was three.
He drifted west to Texas and tried almost everything — ranch hand, pharmacist, mapmaker, bank clerk — and none of it quite fit.
Then the bank's money did not add up. In eighteen ninety-six, Porter was charged with taking money from the bank where he worked in Austin.
The day before his trial, he panicked and ran — all the way to Honduras. He only came home because his wife was dying, and he reached her in time to say goodbye.

The court found him guilty, and he spent just over three years in the state prison in Columbus, Ohio. He always insisted the accounts were a muddle, not a theft — but he had run, and running looks like guilt.

Here is the strange part: prison is where the writer was born. He wrote stories in his cell at night and posted them to magazines under invented names, so that nobody would know they came from a prisoner.
One of those invented names was O. Henry. Nobody is completely sure where it came from — one story says he borrowed it from a prison guard called Orrin Henry.
In nineteen-oh-two he moved to New York, and the city poured straight into his notebooks. A newspaper paid him to write one story every single week — and for over a year, he did.

He wrote nearly four hundred stories in his short life, almost all with a surprise waiting in the last paragraph. Readers began buying them just to see if they could guess the ending. They usually could not.
The money came fast and left faster. He was generous, he drank too much, and in nineteen ten he died in New York, aged forty-seven, famous and nearly broke.
Nine years later, America named its most important short-story prize after him — the O. Henry Award. The man who once hid his name now has writers competing to win it.

So remember, when you read this story about a poor young couple in a cheap New York flat: he was not imagining that life. He knew being poor, he knew losing everything — and he knew, better than almost anyone, how to start again.
ohenry.html:
Who he was

Two namesO. Henry was the pen name of William Sydney Porter (1862–1910), an American short-story writer. He is remembered above all for one thing: the surprise ending — a final paragraph that turns the whole story upside down, fairly, using only what you had already been shown. He wrote nearly 400 stories, most of them about ordinary people: shop girls, clerks, policemen, and young couples with almost no money.

The trouble in Texas

The dark chapterAs a young man Porter worked as a clerk in a bank in Austin, Texas. The accounts were found to be short, and he was charged with embezzlement — taking money that was not his. He fled to Honduras rather than face trial, but returned when his wife was dying of tuberculosis. In 1898 he was convicted and sent to the state prison in Columbus, Ohio. He served just over three years of a five-year sentence. Whether he truly stole, or was simply careless with badly kept books, is still debated — but the running away did not help his case.

The writer born in prison

The turnIn prison he began writing stories seriously and sent them to magazines under false names, hiding the fact that the author was a prisoner. The name "O. Henry" first appeared on a story in 1899, while he was still inside. Nobody knows for certain where the name came from — one popular account says he took it from a prison guard named Orrin Henry, but there are other theories, and Porter enjoyed never quite explaining it.

New York, a story a week

The famous yearsIn 1902 he moved to New York City, the setting of this story, and became astonishingly productive. The New York World's Sunday magazine paid him to deliver one story every week, and for over a year he kept that pace. He called New York's ordinary people "the four million" — everyone, not just the rich few — and made that the title of his 1906 collection, which includes The Gift of the Magi.

"It was a modest little story about being poor at Christmas — and it became one of the most retold stories on earth."On "The Gift of the Magi", first published December 1905

The end, and the afterlife

1910Fame did not make him careful. He earned well, gave money away, drank heavily, and died in New York in 1910, aged 47, with very little left. In 1919 the annual O. Henry Award — still one of America's most respected short-story prizes — was founded in his memory. The man who once hid his name from editors now has his name on the prize.

Why this matters for the story

The connectionJim and Della live in a cheap flat, count pennies, and lose their most precious things — and the story never once looks down on them. Porter had been poor, disgraced, and imprisoned, and he had started his life over from a prison cell. When he writes about people who have almost nothing and give it away anyway, he writes as someone who knew being poor, and knew starting again.

impact.title: One Story, Everywhere
impact.caption: About four pages long. Translated, filmed, retold — and still going.
spoken: This story is about four pages long. It was written for one Sunday newspaper, for one Christmas, in nineteen-oh-five — and it has never stopped being retold since.
Part of the reason is the ending, which is so famous it is taught with its own name: situational irony — when what actually happens is the exact opposite of what everyone expected.

Each gift is perfect, and each gift arrives useless — and somehow that makes the story happier, not sadder. Very few endings manage both at once, and this one has been the classroom example for a century.
The title itself has entered the language. When two people each give up their own treasure for the other, English speakers call it 'a gift of the magi' situation — no explanation needed.

It may be one of the most widely taught short stories in the world. It is short, the words are simple, and the ending needs no translation — so it sits in school books from Japan to Brazil to your own classroom, right now.
It has been adapted almost without pause: silent films over a century ago, then musicals, an opera, and television — even The Simpsons, Sesame Street and Futurama have borrowed its ending.
Every Christmas, somewhere, a newspaper retells it, a radio station reads it aloud, and a sitcom quietly steals its plot. Borrowing this story has become a tradition of its own.
Not everyone admires it. Some critics call the ending a clever trick — a machine for producing tears. That is worth debating: does a story become less true because it is perfectly built?
But here is the test the story keeps passing: you already know the ending, the whole world knows the ending — and it still works.
A tiny story about two poor people and two useless gifts, still travelling the world a hundred and twenty years later. That is what happens when a writer gets the ending exactly right.
impact.html:
The short version

Small story, long life"The Gift of the Magi" first appeared in the New York Sunday World on 10 December 1905, filling part of one Christmas page. Legend says O. Henry wrote it in a few hours, right on deadline — Pete's Tavern in New York still shows visitors the booth where it supposedly happened, though nobody can prove the story was written there rather than in his flat nearby. Whatever the truth of the legend, the result is one of the most retold short stories in the English language.

The twist with a name

Situational ironyThe ending is so famous that teachers use it to define a term: situational irony — when what happens is the opposite of what was expected. Della sells her hair to buy a chain for Jim's watch; Jim sells the watch to buy combs for Della's hair. Each gift is perfect, and each arrives useless. The deeper twist is that the story insists this is not a failure at all: the useless gifts are the proof of love. That double turn — ironic and warm — is why the ending is studied rather than just enjoyed.

Into the language

A phrase, not just a titleThe title has become shorthand. When two people each sacrifice their own treasure for the other — and the sacrifices cancel out — English speakers call it a "gift of the magi" situation. Economists, advice columnists and headline writers all use the phrase without explaining it. Very few stories become an expression.

In classrooms everywhere

It is short

About four pages. It fits in any textbook, any lesson, any language course — which is one honest reason it is taught so widely.

It is simple on the surface

Plain words, two characters, one flat, one problem. Learners of English can read it early — and still find something underneath.

The ending needs no translation

The irony survives every language it enters, which is why the story appears in school books across the world.

Adaptations without end

Borrowed everywhereThe story has been adapted since the era of silent film — versions exist from as early as 1909 — and it has never stopped: Hollywood films, stage musicals, a 2019 chamber opera by Eric Whitacre, and countless television episodes. Sesame Street, The Honeymooners, The Simpsons and Futurama have all retold or reworked its ending. Borrowing this plot at Christmas has become a television tradition in itself.

A fair criticism

The other viewSome critics find the story too neat — a tear-producing machine, engineered to ambush the reader. That is a reasonable charge, and worth arguing about. But the story has one strong answer: almost everyone now knows the ending before they read it, and it works anyway. A trick you can see coming, that still moves you, may be something better than a trick.

guideVoice.name: Wren
guideVoice.hello: You're back! Or you're new — either way, good. This one isn't scary, I promise. It's about two people who are broke and in love, the day before Christmas. Pick a reading and we'll start — or sign in with your class first, if your teacher sent you.

passIntro.1: First time through, you just watch. It's short — and nobody dies. But somewhere in the middle your stomach is going to drop. Don't say I didn't warn you.
passIntro.2: Round two. Before each part I'll tell you one thing to look for, then I'll ask you about that exact thing. This story hides things in plain sight, so — eyes open.
passIntro.3: Last one, the real one. You write. Your own words, actual sentences. And the last question is a big one, so save some thinking for it.

praise: Good — that's the bit that matters.
nudge: Close. Read the line once more.
The answer is in the line itself. Have another look.

end.1: That's the whole story. One dollar eighty-seven, two treasures, two gifts. Now we go back through slowly, and this time I get to talk.
end.2: Good. You saw the trick coming the second time, didn't you? That's the strange thing — it gets better when you know. Now the hard one: your words.
end.3: Done. Three times through. And if anybody ever asks you what irony means, you can just tell them this story in one breath. That's yours now.

s1.line: Three times. She counted it three times.

s2.line: Twenty dollars a week, and she still hugs him at the door.

s3.line: A gray cat on a gray fence. Even the cat is broke.
She's decided something. Look at her face.

s4.line: Two tears. That's all she lets herself have.

s5.line: Quick — before she can change her mind.

s6.line: Quiet and valuable. She's describing Jim.

s7.line: What could I do. Remember that question.

s8.line: Make him think I am still pretty. Oh, Della.
That's not anger. What IS that?

s9.line: Nobody could ever count my love for you.

s10.line: The combs. For the hair. Oh no.
Wait — she just remembered HER present.

s11.line: He says it lying down. Smiling. That's the whole man.

s12.line: They are the magi. Last three words, and it's the title.

preshow.text: Okay. This is The Gift of the Magi. Nineteen-oh-five, New York City, the day before Christmas. Two people, one tiny flat, and one dollar and eighty-seven cents.
It's short. You could read it in ten minutes. And it has maybe the most famous ending of any short story in the world — people quote it who have never read it.
The man who wrote it called himself O. Henry. That wasn't his real name, and there's a reason, and it's a good story — but it can wait until the author page.
Here's what I want you to hold on to: he knew exactly what being broke feels like. The counting, the pretending, the shame at the shop counter. He isn't guessing.
Quiet now. You don't have to do anything. Professor Ambrose reads, the pictures move, and somewhere in the middle your stomach is going to drop. That's supposed to happen.
I'm watching it with you. And when you get to the last line — that's my favourite last line anywhere, so don't talk over it.

s3.label: Looking back — Act I
s3.q: Across these first three parts, what has actually happened?
opts: Della has sold her hair and bought Jim's present.
Jim has come home early and found Della crying on the couch.
Della has counted her money, cried, and decided something she has not told us yet.
Della has borrowed the money she needs from the shopkeepers.
s3.fb: One dollar and eighty-seven cents, counted three times. A cry on the shabby couch. Then shining eyes at the mirror, and her hair let down to its full length. We have watched her decide — but nobody has said what the decision is.
s3.wren: Count, cry, mirror. She's decided something and the story won't tell us what. That's why you can't stop here.

s6.label: Looking back — Act II
s6.q: Across this act, what has Della actually traded — and for what?
opts: Her months of small savings, in exchange for Jim's gold watch.
One of the two treasures of the house, to be worthy of the other.
Her old brown jacket and hat, for twenty-one dollars in a shop.
Nothing yet — she is still standing in front of the mirror, deciding.
s6.fb: The house holds two treasures: the watch and the hair. She sold hers to buy something 'even worthy of The Watch'. That is half of a shape — keep hold of it.
s6.wren: She sold one treasure to dress the other one. Hold that shape in your head. It's going to matter.

s9.label: Looking back — Act III
s9.q: During the long stare at the door, what does Jim know that Della does not — and that we, the readers, do not know yet either?
opts: That her hair is gone forever and will never grow back.
That he has lost his job and cannot buy her anything at all.
That the gift in his pocket was made for the hair she has just sold.
That Della has been hiding money from him all through the year.
s9.fb: His stare is 'not anger, nor surprise... nor horror' — he is holding combs for hair that no longer exists. We only find that out one scene later, and then the stare makes perfect sense.
s9.wren: He's not angry. He's doing a sum in his head that we can't see yet. Once you know about the combs, go back and read the stare again. It's a different scene.

s12.label: Looking back — the whole story
s12.q: Look at the shape of the twist. What do the two gifts do to each other?
opts: Each gift points at the treasure the other person gave up.
Each gift turns out to be worth more money than they paid for it.
Jim's gift ruins the evening and Della's gift saves it.
The two gifts cancel out, so nothing in the story has really changed.
s12.fb: A chain for a watch that is sold; combs for hair that is cut. Both gifts are useless — and both are perfect, because each one says: I gave up my best thing for you.
s12.wren: Two useless presents. And they're the two most perfect presents in any story I know. Both of those things are true at the same time. That's the whole trick.

s1.text: Okay, but why doesn't she just not buy him a present? He'd understand. They're broke.
He would understand. That is exactly the problem. She has spent months planning something fine for him — giving up now would mean the money won.
So she counts it again. Like it's going to be different the third time.
She knows it will not be. Hold on to that number — one dollar and eighty-seven cents. The whole story is going to balance on it.

s2.text: Why is the narrator making jokes about their doorbell? She's upstairs crying.
He steps away to let her cry in private, and shows us the flat instead. A letter-box no letter fits, a bell no finger can ring — and above them, a long proud name on a card.
The card's a bit sad, honestly. Thirty dollars a week and a big fancy name, and now...

Now twenty, and the name is thinking of shrinking to match. But notice the one thing that has not shrunk — she still hugs him at the door every evening. The narrator calls that 'all very good'. Ask yourself what he means by it.

s3.text: Everything out that window is gray. He says gray three times in one sentence.
On purpose. A gray cat on a gray fence in a gray backyard — the world offering her nothing at all. And then she turns to the mirror, and her eyes are the one bright thing in the room.
But her face goes white. In twenty seconds. That's fast.
Shining eyes and a pale face in the same moment — excitement and fear together. Now watch her hands. What she does with her hair tells you what she has decided, before anyone says it out loud.

s4.text: The queen of Sheba living across the airshaft. That's ridiculous.

Deliberately ridiculous. The narrator exaggerates like a friend boasting for them — a queen would envy Della's hair, a king would envy Jim's watch. Two people with a broken doorbell, and treasures royalty would want.
And then she puts her hair up again, fast, and two tears fall on the carpet.
She falters exactly once, and then she moves. Keep both treasures in your mind — the watch and the hair. The story is about to weigh one against the other.

s5.text: Twenty dollars. She doesn't even argue. She just says give it to me quick.
Quick is the important word. If she stands there holding her own hair, she may find she cannot sell it after all.
And the shop woman doesn't care at all. It's just... stock, to her.
Not at all. Madame is chilly; Della's eyes are sparkling. Watch that difference — the same hair, and it means two completely different things.

s6.text: She found it! Two hours, every store in town, and it's — a chain. A plain little chain.
A plain platinum chain, with no ornament at all. The narrator says its value comes from substance, not from show.
'Quietness and value.' That's how you'd describe a person, not a chain.
It is exactly how you would describe one person in this story. And look at the last lines — a grand watch on an old leather strap. Ask yourself why Jim checks the time secretly.

s7.text: Forty minutes with the curling irons. The excitement's gone. She's scared now, isn't she.
The mirror is honest, and she knows it. She calls her own reflection a schoolboy and a chorus girl in the same minute.
'What could I do.' She says it twice. Like she's asking someone.
One dollar and eighty-seven cents — the number from the very first line of the story. When she asks that question, ask yourself who all of this was for.

s8.text: He just... stops. In the doorway. And stares at her.
And notice what the narrator does first — he tells us Jim is twenty-two, needs a coat, and has no gloves. Three small, poor facts. Keep them.
She had a whole list ready. Anger, surprise, horror. And it's none of them.
None of them. We know one thing Jim does not — the chain doubled in her hand. And Jim knows one thing we do not — why he is staring. Hold both, and turn the page.

s9.text: He keeps asking the same question. 'You've cut off your hair?' He heard her the first time.
He heard her. But he is doing a sum in his head that she cannot see, and the answer keeps coming out impossible.
And she thinks he's angry with her. She's standing there asking him to still like her.
He is not angry. He is carrying a secret of his own up those stairs. The next part opens it — for now, just notice that the narrator promises to explain his strange riddle 'later on'.

s10.text: Combs. For the hair she just sold. That is so cruel.
Cruel of whom? Nobody in that room did anything except love the other one. The cruelty is all in the timing.
And she's the one crying, and she still says her hair grows fast. She's comforting him.
That small sentence is plain bravery. And watch her leap up at the end — she has just remembered that this evening has a second present in it.

s11.text: 'I sold the watch to get the money to buy your combs.' He just says it. One sentence, no warning.
Flat as a train timetable. O. Henry hides the biggest sentence of his story inside the smallest voice he has.
And then he asks her to cook dinner. After that.
'Suppose you put the chops on.' Everything is lost, and nothing is lost, and dinner still needs cooking. Ask yourself why that ordinary line is the tender one.

s12.text: He calls them foolish children and then the wisest of everyone. In the same paragraph. Which is it?
Both, perhaps. He says the gifts were foolish and the givers were wise. Those are two different measurements, and he wants you to hold them apart.
And the very last word of the whole story is the title. 'They are the magi.'
He kept it wrapped until the end, like a gift. Now it is your turn to judge them: foolish or wise. Either answer is allowed — if you can defend it with lines from the story.

ohenry.text: Wait — he actually went to prison? For stealing? And we're still supposed to like him?

He was convicted of taking money from the bank where he worked, and he served just over three years. He always said the books were a mess rather than a theft — but he ran away before the trial, and that was his real mistake. I will not pretend it did not happen.
So is it okay to like his stories?

You are not being asked to decide he was a good man — only to read what he wrote. And notice what he did with those three years: he sat in a cell and taught himself to write. The stories are what he made of the worst thing that ever happened to him.
So the man writing about people with nothing... had actually been the man with nothing.
Exactly. Hold on to that. Jim and Della count pennies, and the story never once laughs at them. That kindness comes from somewhere.

impact.text: The Simpsons did this story? The actual Simpsons?
The Simpsons, Sesame Street, Futurama, films going back over a century, even an opera. Stealing this ending at Christmas is practically a tradition.
But if everyone already knows the twist... doesn't that ruin it?

That is the interesting part. A twist that only works once is a trick. This one is something else — the surprise wears off, and what the gifts prove does not. That is the question I want you to write about.

es: Un dólar y 87 centavos.

Y 60 centavos estaban en monedas de un centavo.
Monedas ahorradas de una en una y de dos en dos,

Lo cual nos lleva a la reflexión moral
de que la vida se compone de sollozos, lloriqueos y sonrisas,
con los lloriqueos en primer lugar.

es: Mientras la señora de la casa pasa poco a poco de la primera etapa a la segunda,
echemos un vistazo a la casa.
Un departamento amueblado de 8 dólares por semana.
No era exactamente indescriptible de tan pobre,
pero sin duda estaba a un paso de parecer un lugar de mendigos.
En el vestíbulo de abajo había un buzón donde no entraba ninguna carta,
y un timbre eléctrico del que ningún dedo humano podía sacar un sonido.
También había allí una tarjeta con el nombre
"Sr. James Dillingham Young".
El "Dillingham" se había lucido al viento
durante una época anterior de prosperidad,
cuando su dueño ganaba 30 dólares por semana.
Ahora que el ingreso había bajado a 20 dólares,
pensaban seriamente en reducirlo a una modesta y humilde D.
Pero cada vez que el Sr. James Dillingham Young llegaba a casa y subía a su departamento,
la Sra. James Dillingham Young lo llamaba "Jim" y lo abrazaba con fuerza,
ella, a quien ya les presenté como Della.
Y todo eso está muy bien.

还有一个电铃按钮,却没有人的手指能把它按响。
那里还挂着一张名片,上面写着
"詹姆斯·迪林厄姆·杨先生"。
这个"迪林厄姆"是从前风光的时候大大方方亮出来的,
那是在以前日子好过的时期,
当时它的主人每周能挣30美元。
可现在收入缩水到了每周20美元,
他们正认真考虑把它缩写成一个低调朴素的"迪"字。
不过,每当詹姆斯·迪林厄姆·杨先生回家走进楼上的公寓时,
詹姆斯·迪林厄姆·杨太太总是叫他"吉姆",并紧紧地拥抱他。
这位太太就是前面介绍过的德拉。
这一切都非常好。
vi: Trong lúc cô chủ nhà đang dần dịu xuống, từ khóc òa chuyển sang sụt sịt,
ta hãy nhìn qua căn nhà một chút.
Một căn hộ có sẵn đồ đạc, giá thuê 8 đô la một tuần.
Nó chưa đến mức nghèo không tả nổi,
nhưng chắc chắn trông cũng chẳng khác nơi ở của người đi ăn xin là bao.
Dưới lối vào có một thùng thư mà chẳng lá thư nào chịu chui vào,
và một nút chuông điện mà không ngón tay người nào bấm ra nổi tiếng chuông.
Ở đó còn gắn một tấm thẻ ghi tên
"Ông James Dillingham Young".
Cái tên đệm "Dillingham" từng được trưng ra đầy kiêu hãnh
vào thời còn khấm khá trước kia,
khi chủ nhân của nó được trả 30 đô la một tuần.
Nhưng bây giờ, khi thu nhập đã co lại còn 20 đô la,
họ đang nghĩ nghiêm túc đến chuyện rút gọn nó thành một chữ D khiêm tốn, giản dị.
Nhưng mỗi khi ông James Dillingham Young về nhà và lên đến căn hộ của mình
anh được gọi là "Jim" và được bà James Dillingham Young ôm chầm lấy,
người mà các bạn đã biết, chính là Della.

id: Sementara nyonya rumah perlahan mereda dari tahap pertama ke tahap kedua,
mari kita lihat-lihat rumahnya.
Sebuah flat berperabot dengan sewa 8 dolar seminggu.
Tempat itu belum sampai miskin tak terlukiskan,
tetapi jelas tampak nyaris seperti tempat tinggal pengemis.
Di ruang masuk bawah ada kotak surat yang tak pernah kemasukan surat,
dan sebuah bel listrik yang tak bisa dibuat berbunyi oleh jari manusia mana pun.
Di situ juga terpasang sebuah kartu bertuliskan nama
"Tuan James Dillingham Young".
Nama "Dillingham" itu dulu dipajang dengan bangga
pada masa makmur yang telah lewat,
ketika pemiliknya digaji 30 dolar seminggu.
Tetapi sekarang, ketika penghasilan menyusut menjadi 20 dolar,
mereka berpikir serius untuk menyingkatnya menjadi huruf D yang sederhana dan rendah hati.
Namun setiap kali Tuan James Dillingham Young pulang dan sampai di flatnya di atas,
ia dipanggil "Jim" dan dipeluk erat-erat oleh Nyonya James Dillingham Young,
yang sudah diperkenalkan kepada kalian sebagai Della.
Dan itu semua sungguh baik.
pt: Enquanto a dona da casa vai passando aos poucos da primeira etapa para a segunda,
vamos dar uma olhada na casa.
Um apartamento mobiliado de 8 dólares por semana.
Não era exatamente pobre demais para descrever,
mas com certeza estava a um passo de parecer coisa de mendigo.
No vestíbulo, embaixo, havia uma caixa de correio onde carta nenhuma entrava,
e uma campainha elétrica da qual nenhum dedo humano conseguia arrancar um toque.
Havia ali também um cartão com o nome
"Sr. James Dillingham Young".
O "Dillingham" tinha sido exibido ao vento
durante uma época anterior de prosperidade,
quando seu dono ganhava 30 dólares por semana.
Agora que a renda tinha encolhido para 20 dólares,
eles pensavam seriamente em reduzi-lo a um modesto e humilde D.
Mas sempre que o Sr. James Dillingham Young chegava em casa e subia ao apartamento,
ele era chamado de "Jim" e recebia um grande abraço da Sra. James Dillingham Young,
que já apresentei a vocês como Della.
E isso tudo é muito bom.
fr: Pendant que la maîtresse de maison passe peu à peu de la première étape à la deuxième,
regardons le logement.
Un appartement meublé à 8 dollars par semaine.
Il n'était pas exactement misérable au point d'être indescriptible,
mais il n'était vraiment pas loin d'attirer la brigade anti-mendicité.
Dans l'entrée, en bas, il y avait une boîte aux lettres où aucune lettre ne pouvait entrer,
et un bouton de sonnette dont aucun doigt humain ne pouvait tirer un son.
Il y avait aussi une carte portant le nom
« M. James Dillingham Young ».
Le « Dillingham » avait été affiché fièrement
pendant une période passée de prospérité,
quand son propriétaire gagnait 30 dollars par semaine.
Mais maintenant que le revenu était tombé à 20 dollars,
ils pensaient sérieusement à le réduire à un simple et modeste D.
Mais chaque fois que M. James Dillingham Young rentrait chez lui et arrivait à son appartement,
il était appelé « Jim » et serré très fort dans les bras de Mme James Dillingham Young,
que je vous ai déjà présentée sous le nom de Della.
Et tout cela est très bien.
ru: Пока хозяйка дома постепенно переходит от первой стадии ко второй,
осмотрим сам дом.
Меблированная квартирка за 8 долларов в неделю.
Нельзя сказать, что она была совсем нищенской,
но слово «нищета» явно было где-то совсем рядом.
В подъезде внизу был почтовый ящик, в который не пролезло бы ни одно письмо,
и кнопка звонка, из которой ни один смертный палец не смог бы выжать ни звука.
Там же висела карточка с именем:
«Мистер Джеймс Диллингхэм Янг».
Слово «Диллингхэм» появилось там с размахом
в прежние времена достатка,
когда его владелец получал 30 долларов в неделю.
Теперь, когда доход сократился до 20 долларов,
они всерьёз подумывали сократить его до скромного и незаметного «Д».
Но всякий раз, когда мистер Джеймс Диллингхэм Янг приходил домой и поднимался в свою квартиру,
его называли «Джим» и крепко обнимала миссис Джеймс Диллингхэм Янг,
уже известная вам как Делла.
И это очень хорошо.

es: Della terminó de llorar y se arregló las mejillas con el paño de los polvos.

a un gato gris que caminaba por una cerca gris en un patio gris.
Mañana sería el día de Navidad,
y ella solo tenía 1.87 dólares para comprarle un regalo a Jim.
Llevaba meses ahorrando cada centavo que podía, con este resultado.
Veinte dólares por semana no alcanzan para mucho.

Siempre lo son.

Algo fino, especial y de verdadera calidad,

de pertenecer a Jim.
Entre las ventanas del cuarto había un espejo largo y estrecho.
Quizás ustedes han visto un espejo así en un departamento de 8 dólares.
